extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent practitioners (attorneys/agents), and others who evaluate patent obviousness under U.S. law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claimed inventions are obvious under 35 U.S.C. § 103, including how to apply Graham factual inquiries, motivation/suggestion/teaching, common sense, predictable variations, and reasonable expectation of success. Focused on examiner rationale and what findings must be articulated to sustain an obviousness rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common sense may inform obviousness if explained with sufficient reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Common sense has long been recognized to inform the analysis of obviousness if explained with sufficient reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel may invoke common sense but must provide a reasoned explanation and factual foundation supporting use of 'good common sense' rather than conclusory assertions. Case citations: Perfect Web; In re Bozek; In re Zurko; DyStar; In re Kahn. Examples: Board's invocation acceptable when accompanied by reasoned analysis and evidentiary support (B/E Aerospace); unacceptable when no reasoned analysis or record support (Arendi). See MPEP § 2143 regarding need to provide a reasoned explanation even in situations involving common sense or ordinary ingenuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve Graham factual inquiries before using variation-in-fields rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on the rationale that known work in one field may prompt predictable variations for use in another, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After resolving Graham inquiries, examiners must articulate findings (see below) to explain conclusion of obviousness. The relevant time for analysis depends on AIA/pre-AIA status (before effective filing date vs. time of invention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Findings required for design-incentives/market-forces rationale (five findings)
rubrics_metrics.description: When asserting that design incentives or market forces would have prompted predictable adaptation of prior art, Office personnel must articulate five findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The five required findings: (1) scope and content of the prior art included a similar or analogous device (method, or product); (2) there were design incentives or market forces which would have prompted adaptation of the known device (method, or product); (3) differences between the claimed invention and the prior art were encompassed in known variations or in a principle known in the prior art; (4) one of ordinary skill, in view of the identified design incentives or market forces, could have implemented the claimed variation and it would have been predictable to that artisan; and (5) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary to explain a conclusion of obviousness. If any finding cannot be made, this rationale cannot support obviousness. Examples: Dann v. Johnston; Leapfrog; KSR; Ex parte Catan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation (TSM) to modify/combine references must be articulated
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness can be established by combining or modifying prior art teachings where there is some teaching, suggestion, or motivation to do so; examiners must articulate such TSM findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required findings for TSM-based rejections: (1) a finding that there was some teaching, suggestion, or motivation (in the references or knowledge generally available) to modify or combine; (2) a finding that there was a reasonable expectation of success; and (3) additional Graham-based findings as necessary. The motivation to combine can be explicit or implicit (market forces, design incentives, interrelated patent teachings, known problems in the field, background knowledge, creativity, common sense). Case law: In re Kahn; DyStar; Plantronics; Zup; KSR; Axonics. The TSM test is flexible—an explicit written motivation is not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success is required
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable expectation of success in making the modification or combination is required to establish obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The relevant time for evaluating expectation is before the effective filing date (AIA/FITF) or at the time of the invention (pre-AIA). Examiners must show that a person of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation that the modification/combination would work. See MPEP § 2143.02 and cases such as In re Kahn and Axonics. Lack of reasonable expectation undercuts obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of desirable alternatives does not necessarily teach away
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art disclosure of multiple alternatives or a more desirable alternative does not automatically negate a suggestion to modify or combine to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference does not teach away merely by disclosing more than one alternative; teaching away requires criticism, discrediting, or discouragement of the claimed solution. Examples: In re Fulton (desirable alternatives not teaching away); In re Urbanski; Ruiz v. A.B. Chance Co. Examiner should consider whether the prior art as a whole suggests the desirability of the claimed combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: When prior art teachings conflict, weigh the suggestive power of each reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Where teachings of two or more prior art references conflict, the examiner must weigh the suggestive power of each reference to one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the degree to which one reference discredits another and evaluate teachings across analogous arts. Example: In re Young—subsequent article did not sufficiently deter use of earlier patent teachings because conditions were not comparable. Examiners must analyze which teachings would have suggested the solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere ability to combine/modify references is insufficient unless variation would have been predictable
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that references can be combined or modified does not render the result obvious unless the results would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite KSR: if an artisan can implement a predictable variation, §103 likely bars patentability; unpredictability may defeat obviousness. Examiner must show predictability, not just theoretical combinability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusions that the claimed invention is within ordinary skill are insufficient without articulated reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere statement that modifications would have been 'well within the ordinary skill of the art' is not sufficient to establish a prima facie case of obviousness absent objective reasons to combine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections must avoid conclusory statements and must include articulated reasoning with rational underpinning. Cases: Ex parte Levengood; KSR; In re Kahn. Provide factual/supporting explanation rather than generic assertions about skill level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed modification cannot render the prior art unsatisfactory for its intended purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proposed modification would make the prior art device inoperable or unsatisfactory for its intended purpose, there may be no suggestion or motivation to make the proposed modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Gordon—turning the reference device upside down would have made it inoperable. However, courts have sometimes found that tradeoffs (advantages/disadvantages) do not necessarily obviate motivation to combine (Allied Erecting v. Genesis Attachments). Examiner must analyze whether the modification would defeat the primary purpose taught by the reference; if so, that weighs against obviousness. See also In re Dance and Medichem citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed modification cannot change the principle of operation of a reference
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proposed modification or combination would change the basic principle under which the prior-art reference operates, the teachings are insufficient to render the claims prima facie obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If combination would require substantial reconstruction or redesign and change the principle of operation, the obviousness rejection is improper. Example: In re Ratti (change from rigid to resilient seal required change in principle and reversal of rejection). Examiners must evaluate whether claimed changes alter the operating principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must provide reasoned explanation and factual underpinning to avoid hindsight
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be articulated reasoning with rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This overarching requirement—reiterated throughout KSR and related cases—applies whether relying on common sense, market forces, implicit motivation, or explicit TSM. Examiner should cite evidence, articulate why combinations would have been made, and show reasonable expectation of success. Avoid hindsight reasoning that reconstructs invention from hindsight.
